💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails.
  • According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025.
  • According to recent reports, "The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails.

According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025.

According to recent reports, "The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes.".

"The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft.".

Recent findings suggest that the toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks.

Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed.

A number of aspects make the malware stand apart -.

It has been revealed that the combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data -.

Upon gaining visibility into the email flow, the malware looks for messages containing DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments, and matches at least one of many hard-coded lists with sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject lines, or attachment names.

Emails that meet the filtering criteria are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk, after which they are exfiltrated and deleted via CerealNeuron commands.

In the attack aimed at the Romanian government organization, CerealBox is said to have been configured to gather emails involving NATO and European Union institutional addresses, a pattern that aligns with Russia's strategic priorities.

The commands delivered as compiled .NET programs are handled by CerealRunner, which unpacks and executes the payloads in memory and then sends the results back to CerealNeuron for subsequent exfiltration to the threat actor in encrypted format.

The commands support retrieving mailboxes or specific messages; queuing Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records; running Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries; extracting LSA Secrets; listing volume snapshots; and performing file operations.

"The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands," ESET researcher Matías Porolli said.

"Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that an iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple noted yesterday, and it released updates to fix it.
  • As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.
  • The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must patch to be protected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that an iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple noted yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must patch to be protected.

It has been revealed that the updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

Recent findings suggest that the flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and states different products could use the component.

Recent findings suggest that all nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

According to recent reports, two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

#226. Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (903 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At some point your security will fail.
  • The alert tells you something happened.
  • It has been revealed that people naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in.

The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity.

It has been revealed that people naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right?

Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it?

This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention.

Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you.

The difference in network data indicates up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere.

To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as:.

AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates.

Sources indicate that AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck.

But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system.

As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality.

In a recent development, when evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before.

According to recent reports, these questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go.

In a recent development, detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do?

It has been revealed that your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions.   • The exchange told people to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix.

A researcher who goes by forcequit,  in collaboration with 0xjohnny, released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it.

The exchange told people to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed.

For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions.

Recent findings suggest that the researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container.

He claims the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install.

Recent findings suggest that one of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data.

In a recent development, WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has mentioned whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query.

Sources indicate that the three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range.

Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported".

Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say.

According to recent reports, in a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here.".

The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance owners are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Recent findings suggest that before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Industry observers note that hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

According to recent reports, preview both fields: username demonstrates text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a upcoming scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

Recent findings suggest that at the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:.

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Industry observers note that go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:.

In a recent development, find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:.

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:.

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Sources indicate that preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

Industry observers note that when authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

According to recent reports, in stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

Industry observers note that this is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fireworks AI disclosed on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month  uncovered further malicious activity, affecting account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets, and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts.".

In a recent development, in a notice published on October 10, 2026, the company said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT.

At that time, the AI infrastructure provider stated it only found evidence that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain affected accounts, adding that there were no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information were accessed.

In response to the incident, Fireworks AI took the step of revoking the compromised internal credentials and rotating service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor.

The latest bulletin from the firm reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.

"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use.".

The breach is noted to have provided access to the following types of information -.

Fireworks AI mentioned payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

The manufacturer also noted that it has implemented security hardening procedures, such as credential revocation and rotation; isolating affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement; tightening access controls; and improving its logging and monitoring systems.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to large language models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways," it noted.

The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, which refers to the act of hijacking a victim's LLM through stolen credentials to fuel a criminal enterprise that thrives on peddling the access to other threat actors, while leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill.

Last week, Google issued a warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.

Popular productivity and note-taking application Notion has disclosed that the security incident targeting Fireworks AI impacted "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces." In a post shared on Reddit, one user noted: "looks like all of us are part of that <1%.".

While the initial assessment was that the breach allowed the threat actor to access Notion AI synthetic testing data, it has since come to light that it may also have involved potential customer data.

"Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it mentioned. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.".

According to recent reports, notion has also emphasized that no other features across its platform were affected by the incident. The Insights feature has since been disabled as it continues to investigate the breach and the firm is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

Affected customers are advised to review the impacted data securely inside their workspace. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials during the attack window, it's recommended to rotate them with immediate effect.

Presentation: The Influence Toolkit

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations The Influence Toolkit.

Recent findings suggest that henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence.

Henry Wilson is Senior Architect in the BBC’s Product Group, responsible for backend audio teams. Having worked as a Principal Engineer and Senior Architect at the BBC, he focuses on technical leadership, organizational influence, and senior IC career pathways while guiding complex backend systems and engineering teams.

Recent findings suggest that software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

In a recent development, henry Wilson: I want to start today with a thought exercise. I want you to think about what single skill makes you excel in your current job. I'm sure some of you are thinking about your technical skills, your ability to design architectures, to write code or to solve problems. Maybe some of you are thinking about your research skills, your ability to draw together information from different sources and synthesize it into a plan of action. I'm sure there are many other possible answers that you could have thought of. My view is that if, like me, you're a senior individual contributor at a large organization, the single skill which contributes most to your effectiveness in your role is influence. I would wager that's also true for any of you that hold senior engineering management roles. Let's talk about influence.

Recent findings suggest that I'm a senior architect responsible for the teams in the BBC's audio backend. Just to give a flavor of what those teams do, they deliver the backend functionality for the BBC's audio offering. On BBC Sounds, the BBC's flagship audio experience where they serve an audience of 4.8 million weekly active owners. On third party platforms like Apple and Spotify, where the BBC's RSS platform is responsible for 85 million content downloads a month.

Sources indicate that I'm sure some of you are thinking, why influence? There are many facets to a senior individual contributor role. Why do I want to talk to you about this one? I want to talk to you today about influence, because I've spent a lot of time in the last few years thinking about it. My career at the BBC has seen me move between different roles and different teams, from engineer to senior engineer, then principal engineer, and now architect. In those different roles, I've seen firsthand the power that good influence can have, and what can happen when influence is used in the wrong way. I've also found myself frustrated when I haven't been able to influence a decision in the way that I want to. Why couldn't I persuade that individual or group to adopt the approach I'm suggesting? What could I have done differently that might have led to a different outcome?

Industry observers note that another reason that I want to talk about influence is that it's about communication. Communication really fascinates me. Language is so powerful, so versatile, but also so full of nuance. I love exploring it and understanding how I can make better use of the potential power of my words. The English language leaves an awful lot of room for ambiguity, for accidental implication or for misunderstanding. Ultimately, while senior IC roles are very technical, they're also all about communication. The phrase individual contributor might imply that you sit in a corner on your own being awesome and smashing out contributions, but the reality in large organizations is that you spend far more of your time communicating than you do writing code or creating designs. Even the code that we do write and the designs and documents we create are forms of communication. Ultimately, we're all expressing and communicating ideas all the time in different ways.

Finally, I want to talk about influence because it feels particularly significant for architects. Now, not all organizations have architecture as a separate role from engineering. Some will use senior principal or other staff-plus roles to fulfill a lot of the same duties around technical strategy and technical leadership. At the BBC, architecture sits as a distinct discipline from engineering, which can lead to teams lacking understanding of what architecture's role is and being unsure as to how they should respond if their architect is telling them something they don't understand or is giving them direction that might not match the direction that their colleagues in engineering are giving them. The man in the picture here is the man none of us want to be and none of us want to work with. The architect in the ivory tower handing down their perfect designs, but devoid of context about how those designs will be implemented and become a practical reality.

It has been revealed that they might have influence, but if they do, they're using it in the wrong way. The difference between the ivory tower architect, someone who is likely to be isolated, might be disliked and definitely won't be effective, and the friendly neighborhood architect who the team want to work with and who helps them solve problems is all about communication and all about influence.

It has been revealed that what do we really mean when we talk about influence in the context of senior IC roles? Let's start with this dictionary definition. There are some useful aspects to this, in particular around our ability to have an effect on someone or something, and focusing on the character, development, or behavior of that personal thing. As senior individual contributors, we're often trying to influence behaviors of people or teams, when we want to influence process or ways of working, or we're trying to influence the character and development of the software being built by leading teams to make good technical decisions. Influence is so key to these roles. Without it, it's really hard to be effective in the space. There are likely to be many different targets that you might be trying to influence in different situations. The teams that you have technical responsibility for, the senior leadership in your area, and other disciplines you work with, like product, UX, and architecture or engineering.

Sources indicate that influence for these roles is not the same as managerial authority. Managers still need the ability to influence their staff beyond just saying, I'm your boss, please do as I ask. Nonetheless, there is a reasonable expectation that if your boss asks you to do something, you'll probably do it. Senior IC roles can't rely on that. They need to build reputation with the individuals and teams they're trying to influence. That generally revolves around building relationships. One analogy which I sometimes find useful to consider when we talk about influence is to think of it as a catalyst. We can build our influence by nurturing our relationships, proving ourselves useful to the teams and individuals we work with, being measured in our steer and our interventions. This influence gives us power when significant decisions need to be made and can be used to push technical decision-making forward at key inflection points.

I hope if you give me the benefit of your time today, you'll be able to take a few things away from this talk. Specifically, I intend to give you some tools or techniques you can use to influence the teams and stakeholders you interact with. I'm going to cover my experiences using these tools in different situations. I hope you'll see some parallels with your own teams and projects. You'll ultimately be able to leverage something from this talk to be more effective in your own role.

In a recent development, the project I'm going to focus on for this talk is a large-scale re-architecture within BBC Sounds, which was started around a year ago. This is part of wider org changes to move to the product operating model and start to embrace platform engineering. Why is this project crucial? Because the BBC needs to evolve its digital offering to stay relevant. The BBC's audio offering is a key part of the digital estate and we need to ensure that it's in a fit state to serve the audience. First, I want to cover the project context and the organizational changes at the heart of it. The previous team structure was organized around a product vertical for BBC Sounds. Within that vertical, a catalog team provided core metadata for available audio content. A business-led team consumed that metadata and defined the business logic which powers the BBC Sounds experience. That business logic was used to serve the audience-facing experience across clients on web, mobile, TV devices, and smart speakers.

In a recent development, with the move to platform engineering, this structure needed to change. Under the upcoming structure, the catalog team would sit in platform and the previous business-led team would be split into two halves, one half providing platform APIs. The remaining part of that team would sit within the experiences area of the org, and the audience-facing client teams would also sit within experiences. What would that mean for the split of responsibilities for those new teams? The platform team would own core and personalized metadata with responsibility for creating APIs that describe the catalog of on-demand content, including podcasts, previously aired radio programs, and audiobooks, and live content, the BBC's stable of local and national radio stations. The experience team would own personalization and user experience concerns, building personalized responses based on user context, and owning the logic around experience-specific concerns, such as what content rails are presented in clients, and experience variants, such as the international mode which consumers are presented with when using the app on holiday.

It has been revealed that given that high-level context, I'm now going to drill into some of the complexities around this project and the challenges and opportunities they present when looking at them through the lens of influence. On the technical front, there were various complexities in the BBC Sounds backend landscape to contend with. The technical estate was complex, consisting of over 40 separate microservices with varying degrees of team knowledge and documentation. This is a very zoomed-out view of the estate, just to give you a little flavor of the number of connections and the number of dependencies between different microservices. Some of these key services lacked separation of concerns, mixing personalization, in particular details of user activity, with core API responses. This included the program metadata service, which I'll come back to a little bit more later on. Let's think about those system characteristics, complexity and choices about separation of concerns. We saw in the dictionary definition earlier that influence is about our ability to have an effect on the character of people or things.

Industry observers note that persuading teams to revisit design decisions requires influence. The original estate design prioritized performant responses rather than service decoupling. Additionally, inter-service communication was handled via an RPC implementation using Thrift, built using Finatra and Finagle, which are no longer actively maintained. There was also a desire among platform engineering leadership to move away from the tech stack at the moment used in the estate. Existing services were built using Scala and there was a strong desire to move towards this tech stack that was more commonly used at the BBC due to issues with recruitment, retention, and knowledge sharing. Through our influence lens, this second complexity is about behavior. If we're seeking to change the day-to-day behaviors of a team who are used to using a given set of tools and ask them to learn and use something different, understandably there could be some reluctance to make that change, and this is where our ability to influence becomes key.

Industry observers note that the project also had social complexities. The team had previously operated using a monolithic team structure. There were three engineering teams consisting of 20-plus engineers across dev and test but they'd operated as one large team for over 5 years. There was also an inconsistency around buy-in levels within the team. Attempts to split the team had been attempted before and resisted, and not all members of the existing team were in favor of a split either from a technical point of view or an organizational point of view. Both factors ultimately pointed to a need to try and increase buy-in in order to help with morale and ensure progress on the project. Most social complexities are ultimately about our ability to influence behaviors, and from experience these situations can be really tricky. People problems are almost always harder than technical problems. Finally, there were complexities on the operational front that we needed to consider.

Most significantly this is a high traffic system powering a key audience-facing experience, so there was a need to ensure that the audience experience was not adversely impacted by any of the re-architecture work. On the out-of-hours support front, previously all services had been managed using a single on-call rota leaving a need to consider how to move to clear our ownership boundaries and separate on-call responsibilities across the platform and experience divide but without impacting our operational response. Looked at through our influence lens, again there's a desire to have an effect on system characteristics. We want the system to change but we don't want that to impact the audience, and there is a desire to have an effect on the team's behavior without degrading the operational outcomes.

It has been revealed that given that context, what was my approach? The first steps involved selling the vision to the team. The initial work was to sell the benefits of the change to the team and help them understand why we were doing this. The first key benefit was around increasing the speed of delivery. I'm firmly of the belief that smaller teams with more manageable technical estates can more easily reason about those technical estates and feel confident that they understand everything they're responsible for. This leads to engineers having less fear and greater confidence to evolve the software that they own. Additionally, this change will begin to unlock cross-functional audience experiences which weren't previously possible within the BBC digital estate, such as cross-experience recommendations. Many of you may be fans of "The Traitors," and may also be aware of the companion podcast, "The Traitors: Uncloaked." At present it's not possible to recommend the companion podcast to viewers of the show on iPlayer, and the move towards a platform engineering stance where generic capabilities are exposed to a variety of teams is a key part of breaking down those silos and enabling these richer audience experiences.

I also needed to set expectation with the teams that this change wasn't optional. There was a clear strategy being set by senior leadership and a need to align around that strategy. This kind of project presents key tensions for anyone in an IC role, and that's because those roles rely on building and maintaining strong positive relationships with the teams and individuals you interact with. Operational strategy can't be ignored but the way that you implement that strategy can have a huge impact on your relationships within an organization. This is where we come to the first couple of tools in the influence toolkit. In order to sell the vision, I land on two things. Spoken communication either in person or via video calls is a huge part of the way that we influence people. That spoken communication can be one-to-one or in groups sometimes aided by presenting from slides or talking about documents.

According to recent reports, it's absolutely essential to communicate the vision and build rapport across all levels and disciplines, whether that's engineering, delivery, product, architecture, UX, whatever disciplines you might happen to have in your organization. When I'm speaking to people and trying to sell a vision, I try and make space to allow time for questions and challenges, and to engage honestly with the doubts and fears that individuals might have about what's being proposed. Spoken communication is valuable but it doesn't always scale. If you're trying to influence a group of 30 or even 100, that's an awful lot of one-to-one interactions. This is where context documentation comes in. I led on the creation of context documentation that could be used to disseminate the vision to the wider team, and I collaborated closely with key engineers to outline the problem, the challenges, the rationale, and the planned next steps.

Industry observers note that inevitably, during this vision setting period, there were some areas of pushback from some members of the team and I had to address those. One of the most significant areas of pushback was the view that we didn't have enough idea of future vision or future requirements to inform our approach for changing the technical estate. To address this, I liaised closely with colleagues in product and established that there were no concrete or hypothetical requirements that would be impeded by the proposed approach. Another really significant area of pushback was the view that doing this properly would take three years and anything else would be a bodge. Ultimately, my response to that was quite simple. We don't have the luxury of indulging in 3-year re-architecture projects which don't deliver audience-facing value. Tradeoffs would be required but this change represents an acceptable first step in the evolution of the estate.

When we're thinking about pushback, it can be useful to think about individuals and teams in the matrix of support and resistance. In the top right you've got active supporters. These people are thoroughly bought into whatever you're proposing and whatever you're trying to achieve. They're already cheerleading what you're doing so you shouldn't need to spend any time influencing them, and they should help in your ability to influence others because they're actively supporting your efforts. In the top left you've got passive supporters. They're not so vocal in their support either because they don't care enough or because they're not comfortable evangelizing to a wider team. You shouldn't need to spend that much time influencing here either but you're unlikely to get active help. In the bottom left you'll find passive resistors. They're opposed to your idea or your proposal, but they're not doing anything to really try and prevent things from happening.

In a recent development, passive resistance can have an impact on morale because it can lead to grumbling. It's worth identifying anyone in this camp and spending some time trying to influence them, but they're definitely not the key group. Down in the bottom right you've got the active resistors. They're opposed to the idea or the strategy and they're trying to head in another direction. This can manifest in a few different ways. Active resistance can involve arguing or dissenting in group discussions or in discussions one-to-one, but it can also present in a less obvious way where people say nothing but quietly keep on doing something that doesn't align with the strategy. The active resistors are the group that you should spend most of your time trying to influence, and they will often represent a disproportionately small number of people or teams within your overall sphere of responsibility. If you can influence these individuals to move to passive support or even active support, your ability to drive change will be hugely improved.

Back to the re-architecture. With the team aligned around the vision, the next step was to break down the problem into manageable chunks and identify the key areas that the teams would need to agree approaches for. I collaborated with stakeholders and discipline leads to identify the areas where significant changes would be required and where agreement would need to be reached. That included ways of working, how the teams would interact as they split apart, and how we would approach the work for the re-architecture. How the teams would approach AWS account management given that up until that point all infrastructure resources had been deployed to a single set of accounts. Agreeing ownership of the services in the existing estate between the fresh teams. Agreeing an approach to common libraries and whether there would be a need to adopt an InnerSource model. Looking at a strategy for contract testing to validate the new boundary between platform and experience teams.

Lastly, thinking about how to split functionality in the services at the heart of the estate which needed to change to support the re-architecture. When it comes to achieving consensus, I'm a huge fan of the combined process of RFCs and ADRs, which the teams I was working with in this instance were already familiar with. RFCs, that's request for comment documents, are a powerful starting point for decision-making. I led the creation of an RFC for each significant problem area. The process around RFCs allows for collaboration with key players, and then once you have consensus in a tight group you can widen the group you're seeking input from. This process really empowers good analysis, letting you tease out ideas, gain input, come to consensus, and push decision-making forward. Once each of these RFCs had come to a conclusion, decisions were documented using ADRs. That stands for architecture decision record.

Industry observers note that if anybody isn't familiar with the idea of ADRs I really encourage you to look up this blog post by Michael Nygard. It's an excellent rundown of the concept behind that particular kind of documentation. ADRs provide a perfect format to ensure that key decisions are documented tersely for future reference. Documentation is really powerful but it's not enough on its own. It's also necessary to have regular check-ins with your stakeholders. These can be used to identify any remaining points of contention, have any debates that are still necessary. They provide an opportunity to really push for progress, to ask the group to find the compromise, ask if things are really a problem, and agree an approach so that you can move forward and not get bogged down.

A major part of selling this vision was in helping the teams to understand the long-term strategy but also sending the message that this wasn't the end state, rather a useful stepping stone to allow further evolution of the estate as we evolve the audio offering in line with wider BBC digital looks. Viewing things through that lens, a number of tradeoffs and compromises were accepted. Initially, work on the platform side would create an API on a parity basis, so a newly owned API which provides the same functionality and a very similar API surface to the existing core service. This is probably not the API shape that we would choose if we were designing the API from scratch, and it will undoubtedly require further evolution. Attempting to redesign the API while also splitting the technical estate would have been too complicated and would have introduced unacceptable delays. A greater degree of coupling between platform and experience services than is ultimately desirable will persist for some time after the initial re-architecture work is complete.

Industry observers note that I consider this an acceptable tradeoff to reach a point of separate autonomous teams that are then empowered to further change their technical estates and continue to evolve the system's architecture towards new goals and requirements. A transitionary approach would be required around operational support. Out-of-hours rotas and the handling of business-as-usual maintenance tasks would not be able to immediately match the desired team structures, and this would be necessary to ensure that operational stability wasn't impacted by the re-architecture work.

I can't cover every facet of a project this large, so I'm going to zoom in on some areas where I feel my influence was particularly useful, starting with some decisions around the tech stack used by the platform API team. The team had taken a decision to use Node.js, moving away from Scala. I identified this as an opportunity to leverage the existing approach used in sister teams, such as the catalog team, and I leaned on my experience in those teams where I'd previously laid the foundations of a monorepo approach using CDK for infrastructure and CI/CD. I shared lots of prior art with the new platform team, including code samples and documentation. I conducted targeted knowledge sharing sessions with the team lead and the principal engineer in that space to ensure that they understood the rationale and advantages inherent in the approaches that I was sharing with them.

It has been revealed that I was also influential in guiding the team towards a managed service approach, an opportunity to move away from the maintenance burden associated with running services on EC2, which was heavily used in the previous estate. I suggested that the team should make more use of managed services, such as Lambda and ECS Fargate, and pushed the team to consider the tradeoffs and use the most managed solution wherever possible to keep overheads low, taking a serverless-first approach and only falling back to serverful options where compelling reasons existed. Back to the influence toolkit, these are the techniques that I lean on when I'm working on the ground with teams. Slack is such a valuable tool for collaboration, and it offers really unique opportunities to influence behavior and decision-making. Being present in team channels and observing day-to-day discussions provides valuable opportunities and allows you to spot technical problems or decision points where there might be an opportunity to share prior approaches or leverage existing organizational knowledge.

Slack is so rich. You can link to other Slack conversations, GitHub examples, documentation, blog posts, anything you like. While Slack is a powerful tool, it's really vital that you follow up on those discussions. Speak to the key players and make yourself available to answer questions and dig into the detail. Ultimately, the aim here is to empower the team to use tried and tested patterns as a springboard to deliver faster, but also to upgrade or evolve those approaches where newer libraries or tools might be more powerful.

It has been revealed that the second area I'd like to zoom in on is work around the core program metadata service, which I mentioned earlier on. Before the org change had been announced, work had been planned to remove Thrift from the BBC Sounds estate in order to address security vulnerabilities in the underlying Finatra and Finagle libraries used in the implementation. Due to the complexity of the service implementation, this was many sprints of work for a large number of engineers. That work would ultimately be thrown away in less than a year due to replacement functionality being created in the platform space. Once I'd identified this risk, I raised the issue with senior leadership. There was pushback from the team around the security considerations and the difficulties associated with changing the team's roadmap at short notice. Ultimately, I secured agreement for a change of approach. Once we were further into the re-architecture project, discussions around how to split the core program metadata service began, and the engineers began to think about how far to go with the re-architecture work.

Industry observers note that some of the engineers were keen to look at a larger reimagination of how personalization might work across the estate. I identified this as a source of risk in terms of project timelines. A more complex reimagination could swiftly grow arms and legs, leading to elongated project timelines and blocking any work which could deliver audience value. I pushed strongly for the team to distill options with a focus on simplicity and speed of delivery rather than notions of elegance or wider scope. Not a hack, but a pragmatic path forward.

It has been revealed that some of the discussions around the core program metadata service were difficult, with significant differences of opinion among stakeholders. Perhaps the most key part of the influence toolkit is how we use our influence to have those difficult discussions. Having allies is absolutely essential, whether that's your boss, your peers, or other key stakeholders on the projects that you're working on. That's because the best ideas and the strongest visions will still fail to gain traction if you don't have support, because change is hard. Finally, when approaching tricky discussions, radical candor can be hugely powerful. We need to be willing to have difficult conversations, approach them head-on, and be frank in the way that we address problems. It's important to ensure that we do the right thing, not the easy thing. I'm lifting a quote here from Kim Scott's book entitled, "Radical Candor," caring personally while challenging directly. Scott was talking about management, but I think the same principle applies to influence. If we build a reputation as a caring and empathetic co-worker, we build our influence. When we have good relationships with the people we're trying to influence, then we gain the ability to challenge directly and move discussions forward.

I want to touch on how to measure success. I want to bookend the re-architecture story by covering our progress so far. We're not finished, but we're on track. Agreement has been reached on all the major decision points, and those decisions have all been documented in ADRs for future reference. The platform team have already made a lot of great progress towards creating a latest API surface, and the building experiences to integrate with those new APIs is also underway. Now comes the trickier part, what could have gone better? At times, morale in the team has not felt as high as I might have liked. Change is hard, and there are many factors that affect how people feel, but ultimately this points to an area that I could have had more success. I'm not sure there's any such thing as perfect morale, but that doesn't mean we should ever stop trying to find it.

In a recent development, some of my personal approaches weren't as successful as I'd hoped. Every individual is different, and it often takes time to establish the best way to interact with them. It can be hard to affect positive change when you don't have prior relationships to lean on, or if you're geographically at a distance from the person or team that you're trying to interact with. Sometimes my approach was wide of the mark, and I've tried to learn from those experiences. In terms of buy-in, I think my attempts at vision selling fell short with some members of the team. Now, 100% buy-in is probably unrealistic for a change of any significance, and I remain a big believer in the concept of disagree and commit. Nonetheless, there may have been ways that my vision selling could have been improved.

How do you measure success? How do you tell whether you're any good at influencing the individuals and teams around you? When you're looking to measure your influence around areas of technical complexity, you can track your success by the technical decisions the teams are making. What proportion of those decisions are roughly in line with your desired outcome? How much are those decisions deviating from what you might consider perfect? Reviewing these technical milestones frequently can help you get a feel for the success of your influence. Measuring influence on areas of social and operational complexity is potentially more difficult. You're looking to influence people's behaviors, but behavior can be hard to observe, and individuals won't always be honest about how they truly feel. Outcomes may be harder to track, but you can look for clues. Does morale feel higher? Are you having less difficult conversations? Are you able to classify any of the active resistors you've encountered as passive resistors or as supporters?

Industry observers note that the best thing you can do is ask for feedback. Check in with your stakeholders and your teams. Ask them to give an honest assessment of how you're doing. If you feel brave, you can ask someone you often seem to disagree with to give you feedback. You might find something you can learn from and be able to incorporate into your practice, whether that's positive or negative.

According to recent reports, the nature of feedback and the different ways we can receive it is something I want to touch on, because feedback comes in different forms, and these different signals can help us understand whether our influence is working in the way we want it to. When people think about feedback, they often mean direct feedback. Either you're actively asking someone to tell you how you're doing or to reflect on their interactions with you over the past six months, perhaps. Or someone has something they wish to address with you, and they provide direct feedback without request. Now, that kind of feedback is really useful, especially if you haven't had to ask for it. That means the person you're interacting with really wanted to tell you something, and that's something that you can always learn from, whether it's positive or negative. You can also get some really valuable insights from indirect feedback, and this is where relationships come in.

If you have friendly, positive relationships with the people around you, then the conversations you have can give you valuable indications of the success of your influence. To give an example, I bumped into one of the engineers in the platform API team a few months ago in the office, and I had a short conversation where I asked them how everything was going. They mentioned how positive they'd found the experience of moving into the fresh team structure and using the new tech stack, and how much more rapidly the team were able to build things in this new world compared to their previous experience. These kinds of conversations could easily be dismissed as small talk, where nothing of value is likely to be learned, but in this case, I received an anecdotal indicator. The approach I'd proposed was working for the team. This kind of positive feedback loop, where we make helpful suggestions to teams, is how we build trust and ultimately grow our influence.

Let's recap the tools I've talked about in the influence toolkit. Spoken communication is so powerful. Find opportunities to talk to people, whether that's one-to-one, in groups, over a coffee, in workshops, whatever settings present themselves to you and feel right. Consider context documentation when you're trying to sell a vision to a big team, and use it to scale your influence beyond what can be achieved in one-to-one conversations. Leverage the power of the RFC and ADR process to build consensus and really drive decision-making. Make sure you review regularly with stakeholders around those decisions and keep key players in the loop. Spend time on the ground with your teams. Try and understand the challenges they face, and use tools like Slack to find opportunities to help and guide them. When you share thoughts with your teams in this way, make sure that you follow up. Make time to continue the discussions in the most appropriate way and drill into the detail. Build a network of allies so that your vision is nurtured and you have support when you need it for difficult conversations. Practice radical candor. Build your relationships and be prepared to challenge directly so that you can help your teams to make the right decisions.

Industry observers note that martell: You talked some about how we need to work to get our teams to buy into our vision. Sometimes you're in a place where the vision maybe isn't yours, and you need to get the team to buy into it. Maybe you're not 1,000% aligned. What does that look like? Other than disagree and commit, how do we do that?

Ideally you would get some opportunity to feed into that technical direction. You would have the opportunity to talk to senior leadership and challenge, try and influence the direction that's moving in. I think if you aren't successful in that, if the organization is moving in a direction that you disagree with, you do have to disagree and commit. Either that or you have to find another job. That's a really hard position to be in. I think it asks a lot of people to positively sell a vision they don't truly believe in. I suppose you have to ask yourself how much you disagree with this. I think if you disagree with it too much, then maybe you do need to find another job.

Participant 1: What were the biggest challenges from the active resistors and how you tackled those?

It has been revealed that henry Wilson: I think the challenges in this case were, yes, I think there was a lot of pushback about whether this was something that we really wanted to do and whether it was being pursued for the right reasons. When you're dealing with technical teams that have been in place for a long time, regardless of what job title somebody might have or what seniority they technically hold, people who are long established in teams can have a lot of influence. I think that, yes, that presents challenges if key players are grumbling, and espousing a view that we shouldn't be doing this or that this is a waste of time or that it's doomed to failure in some way.
